title: 535 Farmers Dead from Pesticide Exposure in Two Years. Rajasthan's Assembly Tabled the Numbers.
excerpt: Assembly records reveal a staggering death toll across Rajasthan's farming districts, alongside 189 substandard pesticide samples and wildly unequal compensation payouts.
body:
The numbers, tabled in the Rajasthan assembly, are as blunt as they are damning: 535 farmers dead from pesticide exposure in just two years, between January 2024 and January 2026. Behind the figure lies a lethal intersection of substandard chemicals, absent safety infrastructure, and a compensation system that pays some families and ignores others.

The data, drawn from the state's agriculture department records, maps the toll district by district. Bikaner recorded the highest death count at 57, followed by Churu at 56. Hanumangarh and Jhalawar each reported 42 deaths. Jodhpur recorded 38. Sriganganagar and Beawar reported 31 each.

These are not suicide statistics — a separate and equally grim crisis in Indian agriculture. These are occupational deaths: farmers who died while doing routine agricultural work that involved handling pesticides. The distinction matters, because it points to a systemic failure of regulation, not just economic despair.

## The Compensation Gap

The state government paid ₹5.1 crore in compensation to affected families over the two-year period. On its face, the number suggests the system works. In the details, it falls apart.

Bikaner, with the highest death toll, received ₹92 lakh. Churu received ₹72 lakh. But Jhalawar, despite reporting 42 deaths — exactly as many as Hanumangarh — received only ₹18 lakh, less than half of Hanumangarh's ₹48 lakh payout. Deeg reported eight deaths and received nothing. Kota reported 11 deaths and received ₹2 lakh.

Officials attributed the disparities to differences in "claim verification and approval processes" — bureaucratic language for a system in which whether a dead farmer's family gets paid depends on which district office processes the paperwork.

## Substandard Chemicals in the Supply Chain

Alongside the death data, the assembly received another troubling set of numbers: of 5,570 pesticide samples collected across the state during the same period, 189 failed quality tests. That is a failure rate of roughly 3.4 percent — low enough that officials might dismiss it, high enough that it represents thousands of litres of substandard chemicals entering the fields.

The quality failures suggest that at least some of the 535 deaths were not caused by farmers mishandling safe products. They were caused by farmers using products that should never have reached them.

"If hundreds of farmers are dying while carrying out routine agricultural work, the government cannot wash its hands of responsibility by merely paying compensation," said Kishanpole MLA Amin Kagzi. "We need accountability, stricter regulation of pesticides, and a comprehensive safety programme for farmers across Rajasthan."

## The Diaspora Angle

For NRIs with family ties to Rajasthan's farming communities — and the state sends significant numbers of migrants to the Gulf, the UK, and North America — the data is personal. Many diaspora families maintain agricultural land managed by relatives. The pesticide crisis is not a distant statistic; it is a risk borne by the people they left behind.

India's pesticide regulatory framework has long been criticised for allowing chemicals banned in Europe and North America to remain in domestic use. The problem is compounded by a fragmented supply chain in which counterfeit and substandard products circulate freely, and by a near-total absence of safety training or protective equipment for the farmers who apply them.

The assembly data has not triggered a policy announcement from the Rajasthan government. No new regulations have been proposed. No recall of substandard products has been ordered. The numbers have been tabled, the debate recorded, and the session moved on.

Meanwhile, the monsoon is arriving. Farmers across Bikaner, Churu, Hanumangarh, and Jhalawar will soon return to their fields, handling the same chemicals, in the same conditions, with the same lack of protection that killed 535 of their neighbours in the previous two seasons.
